title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Balashev was used to imperial splendor, but the luxury and magnificence of Napoleon's court still amazed him.

The Comte de Turenne led him into a large reception room, where many generals, gentlemen-in-waiting and Polish magnates were waiting — several of them men Balashev had seen at the Russian Emperor's court. Duroc told him that Napoleon would receive the Russian general before going out for his ride.
A few minutes later the gentleman-in-waiting on duty came into the great reception room, bowed politely, and asked Balashev to follow him.

Balashev went into a small reception room. One of its doors opened into a study — the very one from which the Russian Emperor had sent him on his mission. He stood there a minute or two, waiting. Beyond the door he heard hurried footsteps, and both halves of it were swung quickly open. Then everything went quiet, and from the study came the sound of other steps, firm and resolute. They were Napoleon's. He had just finished dressing for his ride. He wore a blue uniform open at the front over a white waistcoat, which was so long that it covered his rounded stomach, along with white leather breeches that fitted tightly over the fat thighs of his short legs, and Hessian boots. His short hair had plainly just been brushed, yet one lock hung down the middle of his broad forehead. His plump white neck stood out sharply above the black collar of his uniform, and he smelled of Eau de Cologne. His full, rather youthful face, with its prominent chin, wore a gracious and majestic look of imperial welcome.

He came in briskly, jerking with every step, his head slightly thrown back. His whole short, corpulent figure — broad thick shoulders, chest and stomach thrusting forward of their own accord — had the imposing, stately air you see in men of forty who live in comfort. It was also clear that he was in the best of spirits that day.

He nodded in answer to Balashev's low, respectful bow and came straight up to him. He began speaking at once, like a man who prizes every moment of his time, who does not bother to prepare what he will say, and who is sure he will always say the right thing and say it well.

"Good day, General!" he said. "I have received the letter you brought from the Emperor Alexander, and I am very glad to see you." His large eyes glanced into Balashev's face and immediately looked past him.

It was plain that Balashev as a person did not interest him at all. Evidently only what went on in his own mind interested him. Nothing outside himself had any significance for him, because everything in the world, it seemed to him, depended entirely on his will.
"I do not want war, and I never did," he went on, "but it has been forced on me. Even now" (he stressed the word) "I am ready to hear any explanations you can give me."

And he began to set out, clearly and concisely, his reasons for being dissatisfied with the Russian government. The French Emperor spoke in a calm, moderate and friendly tone, and judging by it, Balashev became firmly convinced that he wanted peace and meant to enter into negotiations.

When Napoleon finished and looked questioningly at the Russian envoy, Balashev began a speech he had prepared long before: "Sire! The Emperor, my master..." But the sight of the Emperor's eyes fixed on him threw him into confusion. "You are flustered — compose yourself!" Napoleon seemed to say, as he glanced at Balashev's uniform and sword with a barely noticeable smile.

Balashev recovered and began to speak. He said that the Emperor Alexander did not regard Kurakin's demand for his passports as sufficient cause for war; that Kurakin had acted on his own initiative, without his sovereign's consent; that the Emperor Alexander did not want war and had no ties with England.
"Not yet!" Napoleon cut in. As if afraid of giving vent to his feelings, he frowned and gave a slight nod, a sign that Balashev might go on.

Having said everything he had been instructed to say, Balashev added that the Emperor Alexander wanted peace but would not enter into negotiations except on condition that... Here Balashev hesitated. He remembered the words that the Emperor Alexander had left out of his letter but had specially inserted in the rescript to Saltykov, telling Balashev to repeat them to Napoleon. Balashev remembered these words — "So long as a single armed foe remains on Russian soil" — but some complicated feeling held him back. He wanted to say them and could not. He grew confused and said instead: "On condition that the French army withdraws beyond the Niemen."

Napoleon noticed Balashev's embarrassment as he spoke these last words. His face twitched, and the calf of his left leg began to quiver rhythmically. Without moving from where he stood, he began to speak more loudly and more hurriedly than before. During the speech that followed, Balashev lowered his eyes more than once, and he could not help noticing the quivering of Napoleon's left leg, which grew stronger the more Napoleon raised his voice.

"I want peace no less than the Emperor Alexander does," he began. "Haven't I spent eighteen months doing everything I could to get it? I have waited eighteen months for explanations. But what is demanded of me before negotiations can begin?" he said, frowning and making an energetic questioning gesture with his small, white, plump hand.
"The withdrawal of your army beyond the Niemen, sire," replied Balashev.
"The Niemen?" repeated Napoleon. "So now you want me to retreat beyond the Niemen — only the Niemen?" He repeated it again, looking straight at Balashev.
Balashev bowed his head respectfully.
Four months earlier the demand had been to withdraw from Pomerania; now only a withdrawal beyond the Niemen was asked. Napoleon turned sharply and began to pace the room.

"You say the demand now is that I withdraw beyond the Niemen before negotiations begin. But in exactly the same way, two months ago, the demand was that I withdraw beyond the Vistula and the Oder — and yet you are willing to negotiate."

He walked in silence from one corner of the room to the other, then stopped in front of Balashev again. Balashev saw that his left leg was quivering faster than before and that his face seemed frozen in its stern expression. Napoleon was aware of this quivering of his left leg. "The vibration of my left calf is a great sign with me," he remarked at a later date.

"Demands to retreat beyond the Vistula and the Oder may be made to a Prince of Baden, but not to me!" Napoleon almost screamed, to his own surprise. "If you gave me Petersburg and Moscow, I could not accept such conditions. You say I started this war! But who joined his army first? The Emperor Alexander, not I! And you offer me negotiations when I have spent millions, when you are in alliance with England, and when your position is a bad one. You offer me negotiations! But what is the point of your alliance with England? What has she given you?" He went on hurriedly. He was evidently no longer trying to show the advantages of peace or discuss whether it was possible. He only wanted to prove his own rightness and power, and Alexander's errors and duplicity.

He had plainly begun his speech meaning to show how strong his position was and that he was nonetheless willing to negotiate. But once he started talking, the more he talked, the less he could control his words.
The whole drift of his remarks was now evidently to exalt himself and insult Alexander — exactly what he had least wanted at the start of the interview.
"I hear you have made peace with Turkey?"
Balashev bowed his head in agreement.
"Peace has been concluded..." he began.
But Napoleon would not let him speak. He evidently wanted to do all the talking himself, and he went on with the kind of eloquence and unrestrained irritability that spoiled people are so prone to.

"Yes, I know you have made peace with the Turks without getting Moldavia and Wallachia. I would have given your sovereign those provinces, as I gave him Finland. Yes," he went on, "I promised the Emperor Alexander Moldavia and Wallachia and would have given them to him, and now he won't have those splendid provinces. Yet he could have joined them to his empire and, in a single reign, stretched Russia from the Gulf of Bothnia to the mouths of the Danube. Catherine the Great could not have done more," said Napoleon. He grew more and more excited as he paced up and down the room, repeating to Balashev almost the very words he had used to Alexander himself at Tilsit. "He would have owed all that to my friendship. Oh, what a splendid reign!" he repeated several times. Then he stopped, took a gold snuffbox from his pocket, raised it to his nose, and sniffed at it greedily.
"What a splendid reign the Emperor Alexander's might have been!"
He looked at Balashev with compassion, and as soon as Balashev tried to make some reply, he hastily cut him off.

"What could he wish or look for that he would not have got through my friendship?" demanded Napoleon, shrugging his shoulders in perplexity. "But no, he has preferred to surround himself with my enemies — and with whom? With Steins, Armfeldts, Bennigsens, Wintzingerodes! Stein, a traitor driven out of his own country; Armfeldt, a rake and an intriguer; Wintzingerode, a fugitive French subject; Bennigsen, rather more of a soldier than the others, but all the same an incompetent who could do nothing in 1807, and who ought to awaken terrible memories in the Emperor Alexander's mind.... Granted, if they were competent they might be made use of," Napoleon continued. He could hardly keep pace in words with the rush of thoughts that kept springing up, all proving how right and strong he was (in his mind the two were one and the same). "But they aren't even that! They are fit neither for war nor for peace! Barclay is said to be the ablest of them all, but judging by his first movements I cannot say so. And what are they doing, all these courtiers? Pfuel proposes, Armfeldt argues, Bennigsen considers, and Barclay, called on to act, does not know what to decide, and time passes and brings no result. Bagration alone is a military man. He's stupid, but he has experience, a quick eye and resolution.... And what part is your young monarch playing in that monstrous crowd? They compromise him and make him answerable for everything that happens. A sovereign should not be with the army unless he is a general!" Napoleon said, evidently flinging these words as a direct challenge to the Emperor. He knew how much Alexander wanted to be a military commander.
"The campaign began only a week ago, and you haven't even been able to defend Vilna. You are cut in two and have been driven out of the Polish provinces. Your army is grumbling."

"On the contrary, Your Majesty," said Balashev. He could hardly remember what had been said to him and followed this display of verbal fireworks with difficulty. "The troops are burning with eagerness..."

"I know everything!" Napoleon interrupted. "I know everything. I know the number of your battalions as exactly as I know my own. You do not have two hundred thousand men, and I have three times that many. I give you my word of honor," said Napoleon, forgetting that his word of honor could carry no weight — "I give you my word of honor that I have five hundred and thirty thousand men this side of the Vistula. The Turks will be of no use to you; they are worth nothing, and they have shown it by making peace with you. As for the Swedes, it is their fate to be governed by mad kings. Their king was insane, so they changed him for another — Bernadotte, who promptly went mad — for no Swede would ally himself with Russia unless he were mad."
Napoleon grinned maliciously and again raised his snuffbox to his nose.

Balashev knew how to answer each of Napoleon's remarks and would have done so. Again and again he made the gesture of a man who wants to speak, but Napoleon always cut him off. To the alleged insanity of the Swedes, Balashev wanted to reply that when Russia is on her side, Sweden is practically an island. But Napoleon gave an angry exclamation to drown his voice. Napoleon was in that state of irritability in which a man has to talk, and talk, and talk, merely to convince himself that he is in the right. Balashev began to feel uncomfortable. As an envoy, he feared to demean his dignity and felt he must reply; as a man, he shrank before the fit of groundless rage that had evidently seized Napoleon. He knew that none of the words Napoleon was now uttering meant anything, and that Napoleon himself would be ashamed of them when he came to his senses. Balashev stood with downcast eyes, watching the movements of Napoleon's stout legs and trying to avoid meeting his eyes.
"But what do I care about your allies?" said Napoleon. "I have allies — the Poles. There are eighty thousand of them and they fight like lions. And there will be two hundred thousand of them."

He was probably even more thrown by the fact that he had just told such an obvious falsehood, and that Balashev still stood silent before him in the same attitude of submission to fate. Napoleon abruptly turned round, came close to Balashev's face, and, gesturing rapidly and energetically with his white hands, almost shouted:

"Know that if you stir up Prussia against me, I'll wipe it off the map of Europe!" he declared, his face pale and distorted with anger, and he struck one of his small hands energetically with the other. "Yes, I will throw you back beyond the Dvina and beyond the Dnieper, and I will rebuild against you that barrier which Europe was criminal and blind to let be destroyed. Yes, that is what will happen to you. That is what you have gained by alienating me!" And he walked silently up and down the room several times, his fat shoulders twitching.

He put his snuffbox into his waistcoat pocket, took it out again, raised it to his nose several times, and stopped in front of Balashev. He paused, looked ironically straight into Balashev's eyes, and said in a quiet voice:
"And yet what a splendid reign your master might have had!"

Balashev felt he had to reply, and said that from the Russian side things did not look so gloomy. Napoleon was silent, still looking at him with derision and evidently not listening. Balashev said that in Russia the best results were expected from the war. Napoleon nodded condescendingly, as if to say, "I know it's your duty to say that, but you don't believe it yourself. I have convinced you."

When Balashev had finished, Napoleon took out his snuffbox again, sniffed at it, and stamped his foot twice on the floor as a signal. The door opened. A gentleman-in-waiting bowed respectfully and handed the Emperor his hat and gloves; another brought him a pocket handkerchief. Napoleon turned to Balashev without giving them a glance:

"Assure the Emperor Alexander from me," he said, taking his hat, "that I am as devoted to him as before. I know him thoroughly, and I think very highly of his lofty qualities. I will not detain you any longer, General; you shall receive my letter to the Emperor."
And Napoleon went quickly to the door. Everyone in the reception room rushed forward and down the staircase.
